Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los romances
scenes.desc: El flamenco distingue una docena de palos (romances, tonás, siguiriyas, soleares, tangos, cantiñas, cantes de Levante, fandangos, cantes de Málaga, ida y vuelta, aflamencados e híbridos), cada uno con sus estilos y sus creadores. Los básicos, los más antiguos, empiezan por el romance, la canción española más vieja transmitida oralmente, que los gitanos hicieron suya: es el verdadero punto de origen del cante. También llamados corridos, son las únicas coplas con continuidad narrativa (historias románticas, caballerescas o moriscas) y se cantan a palo seco, sin acompañamiento; con guitarra toman el son de la soleá por bulerías. Washington Irving los oyó en 1829 como «tonadas rudas y sencillas». Hoy casi no se cantan. José Blas Vega grabó en 1971 en el Puerto de Santa María dieciséis romances primitivos de siete intérpretes, todos gitanos, y los dividió en los de flores y Blancaflor, los carolingios, los del Cid, los de Bernardo el Carpio y los moriscos, como el de Zaide; su parentesco con tonás, carceleras, deblas y martinetes es evidente.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: 1958 Percy Phillips Home Recording – "That'll Be the Day" / "In Spite of All the Danger"
facts.body: An ultra-rare, two-sided 78 RPM disc from 1958, recorded by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, pianist John Lowe, and drummer Colin Hanton at the home of Percy Phillips, who specialized in "down and dirty" recordings in his front room. Side one features Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day," and side two contains "In Spite of All the Danger," the first-ever Lennon-McCartney recording. This record is owned by Paul McCartney and is estimated to be worth at least 100,000 pounds if it were ever to be sold. "The result was a two-sided 78 RPM disc with Buddy Holly's That'll Be the Day on Side One, and the first ever Lennon McCartney recording on the other, in spite of all the danger."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Army Enlistment and Rock's Decline (1958)
facts.body: On March 2, 1958, Elvis enlisted in the army, a pivotal moment that led to Rock and Roll losing its "king" and subsequently entering a period of decline that lasted well into the 1960s. "That's the day Elvis enlisted in the army and Rock and Roll lost its king."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Rehiring and Altered Band Dynamics (1958)
facts.body: After performing without Scotty Moore and Bill Black, Elvis realized the live sound wasn't the same and offered them their jobs back. While they received an improved per diem, their roles significantly changed: Bill Black never recorded with Elvis again after the next session, being replaced by Bob Moore in the studio, and Hank Garland became the new lead guitar player on Elvis's records, with Scotty Moore relegated to rhythm guitar. "But after the next recording sessions, Bill never again recorded with Elvis."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Colonel Parker's View of Band Members as Replaceable (1958)
facts.body: The disputes and subsequent changes in Elvis's band solidified Colonel Parker's belief that Scotty Moore and Bill Black were replaceable. He considered them unnecessary for Elvis's continued success in making hit records, a stance that permanently altered Elvis's relationship with his original sidemen. "It was now very clear that the kernel, at least, saw black and Moore as replaceable, and neither of them were necessary for Elvis to continue making hit records."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Colonel Parker's Intent to Remove Leiber and Stoller (c. 1958)
facts.body: Colonel Parker viewed songwriters Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller as a threat ("dangerous") because they commanded Elvis's respect, disliked Parker, were not under his control, and had independent careers. Although they were generating hits and working for RCA, Parker saw them as "loose cannons" and actively sought opportunities to remove them from Elvis's circle. "The two of them were dangerous as far as the kernel was concerned."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Leiber and Stoller's Artistic Frustrations (c. 1958)
facts.body: While Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller liked Elvis personally and admired his work ethic, they found writing for his films to be creatively unfulfilling, not "real art" compared to their R&B work. They considered it "easy money" because anything Elvis recorded sold well, leading to boredom with the routine of producing formulaic songs to "plug into gaps" in his movies. "They didn't have to try too hard to write anything particularly good for him, but they didn't like the kernel, and they were already, after a couple of films, getting bored with the routine nature of writing for Elvis's films."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Rejected "A Walk on the Wild Side" Film Project (c. 1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller proposed a serious film project for Elvis, an adaptation of the novel "A Walk on the Wild Side," set in New Orleans, with producer Charles Feldman and director Ilya Kazan (who had worked with Marlon Brando, one of Elvis's idols). They envisioned this as an opportunity to elevate Elvis's film career, making him respected as both an actor and a singer like Frank Sinatra. This artistic proposition was, however, flatly rejected by Jean Abrabatch of Hill and Range, who warned them against interfering with "the business or artistic workings of the process known as Elvis Presley." "Abrabatch listened to the proposal, called the Colonel to relay the idea, and then said, if you ever try to interfere with the business or artistic workings of the process known as Elvis Presley, if you ever start thinking in this direction again, you will never work for us again."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Leiber and Stoller's Final Separation (June 1958)
facts.body: The collaboration between Elvis and Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller ended permanently after Leiber contracted pneumonia and could not travel for a June 1958 recording session, which Chet Atkins produced. Colonel Parker's insistence on their presence led to Mike Stoller's defiant instruction to Leiber to refuse in strong terms. This incident resulted in Leiber and Stoller never working in the studio with Elvis or being commissioned to write songs for him again. "From this point on, Leighbaugh and Stuller would never work in the studio with Elvis again, and nor would they ever again be commissioned to write a song for him."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Colonel Parker Forces Elvis into the Army (1958)
facts.body: Colonel Parker deliberately manipulated Elvis's military service. He leaked stories to the press alleging "special treatment" for Elvis, then indignantly denied them, ensuring Elvis would serve as a regular soldier rather than in special services, where he could continue his career. Parker's motives included preventing Elvis from devaluing his image with free shows, curbing Elvis's growing independence by isolating him from industry influences in Germany, and making RCA realize their dependence on the Colonel by limiting Elvis's pre-army recording backlog. "Colonel Parker had other ideas."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Private Recordings During Army Service (1958-1960)
facts.body: During his two-year army service, Elvis made no official recordings. The only music he recorded were private sessions with himself and his army friends, captured during their downtime. This lack of a professional backlog was a deliberate strategy by Colonel Parker to exert leverage over RCA. "For the next two years, the only recording Elvis would make would be private ones, of himself and his army friends playing and singing during their downtime."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Mother's Illness and Death (August 14, 1958)
facts.body: Elvis's mother, Gladys Presley, suffered from an illness whose descriptions closely resemble Elvis's own later final illness, leading to speculation about hereditary autoimmune problems. Her condition was potentially exacerbated by diet pills and "fat diets" driven by Colonel Parker's pressure for her to appear thinner in photos with Elvis. She was hospitalized with hepatitis and died on August 14, 1958, at the age of 46, a traumatic event for Elvis who was granted compassionate leave to be with her. "When she died on August 14, aged 46, Elvis was distraught."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Gladys Presley's Funeral and Profound Impact (1958)
facts.body: At Gladys Presley's funeral, Elvis arranged for her favorite gospel quartet, the Blackwood Brothers, to sing "Precious Memories." Her death was arguably the greatest trauma Elvis ever experienced and, even more than his army induction, marked the definitive end of the first phase of his life and career. Her passing removed the only person in his life he could utterly trust, leaving Colonel Parker unchallenged. "Gladys' death, even more than his induction into the army, was the real end of the first phase of Elvis's life in career."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Colonel Parker's Control Solidified (1958)
facts.body: Following Gladys Presley's death and Elvis's forced entry into the army, Colonel Parker faced no remaining obstacles to his complete control over Elvis's career. Gladys had never liked or trusted Parker, but Elvis's father, Vernon Presley, viewed Parker as a necessary business partner, enabling Parker to become the sole, undisputed decision-maker for Elvis's future. "Colonel Parker now had nobody standing in his way."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Private Recordings During Army Service (1958-1960)
facts.body: During his two-year army service, Elvis made no official recordings. The only music he recorded were private sessions with himself and his army friends, captured during their downtime. This lack of a professional backlog was a deliberate strategy by Colonel Parker to exert leverage over RCA. "For the next two years, the only recording Elvis would make would be private ones, of himself and his army friends playing and singing during their downtime."

facts.title: Rehiring and Altered Band Dynamics (1958)
facts.body: After performing without Scotty Moore and Bill Black, Elvis realized the live sound wasn't the same and offered them their jobs back. While they received an improved per diem, their roles significantly changed: Bill Black never recorded with Elvis again after the next session, being replaced by Bob Moore in the studio, and Hank Garland became the new lead guitar player on Elvis's records, with Scotty Moore relegated to rhythm guitar. "But after the next recording sessions, Bill never again recorded with Elvis."

facts.title: Rejected "A Walk on the Wild Side" Film Project (c. 1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller proposed a serious film project for Elvis, an adaptation of the novel "A Walk on the Wild Side," set in New Orleans, with producer Charles Feldman and director Ilya Kazan (who had worked with Marlon Brando, one of Elvis's idols). They envisioned this as an opportunity to elevate Elvis's film career, making him respected as both an actor and a singer like Frank Sinatra. This artistic proposition was, however, flatly rejected by Jean Abrabatch of Hill and Range, who warned them against interfering with "the business or artistic workings of the process known as Elvis Presley." "Abrabatch listened to the proposal, called the Colonel to relay the idea, and then said, if you ever try to interfere with the business or artistic workings of the process known as Elvis Presley, if you ever start thinking in this direction again, you will never work for us again."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Initial Decline in Popularity (1958)
facts.body: Around 1958, rock and roll began its first decline in popularity, marking a point where musical fashions would frequently change, and new artists would regularly replace the most popular acts of the preceding period. This initial decline was notably "traumatic" for the first rock and roll era, characterized by deaths, shifts in fashion, and significant scandals involving figures like Jerry Lee Lewis and Chuck Berry. "We're hitting a point in the history of rock and roll where, for the first time, rock and roll begins its decline in popularity."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Pioneering String Section Use (1958)
facts.body: Buddy Holly was believed to be the first rock and roll singer to record with a full string section when he went into the studio with the Dick Jacobs Orchestra in October 1958. "No rock and roll singer had ever recorded with a full string section before, at least as far as he was aware."

facts.title: Undocumented Period (1958-1964)
facts.body: The period of rock and roll history from 1958 through 1964 is largely undocumented, with many important artists and records of this era receiving little historical attention, often being summarized by the rise of "white bread" pop figures. This neglect is despite the fact that many hits from this time still sound fresh and are staples of oldies radio. "Where currently in a patch of rock and roll history, this is ludicously undocumented."

facts.body: At the time they were writing for Elvis, Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller were employed as staff songwriters for RCA. Despite Colonel Parker's desire to remove them, he allowed them to continue working because they were consistently generating hit songs for the label. facts.title: Colonel Parker's Leverage Against RCA (1958)
facts.body: Colonel Parker intentionally orchestrated Elvis's full military service to limit the creation of a large backlog of recordings for RCA. His strategic goal was to make RCA keenly aware of their dependence on "the Colonel" during Elvis's two-year absence from professional recording. "If he didn't give RCA much of a backlog to release while he was away, RCA would realise how much they needed the Colonel."

facts.title: Scandalous Marriage and UK Tour Downfall (1958)
facts.body: On May 21, 1958, during what was meant to be a triumphant UK tour, Jerry Lee Lewis's career collapsed when the press discovered he had married his 13-year-old cousin, Myra Gale Brown. This revelation, made public upon their arrival in the UK, immediately halted the tour, which was meant to last six weeks but ended after just three days. Lewis's actions, involving a 20-something man marrying a 13-year-old in his own family, were unequivocally deemed "child sexual abuse" and "simply wrong." While Lewis and those around him did not view it as wrong within the context of the Southern US culture at the time, where young marriages to older men were common, this cultural context does not excuse his behavior. His own bass player and Myra's father, J.W. Brown, was so enraged he attempted to murder Lewis with a shotgun, only being deterred by Sam Phillips. "And that is when everything came crashing down, because it was when he and his entourage landed in the UK and the press saw the 13-year-old girl with him and asked who she was that it became public knowledge he had married his 13-year-old cousin, Maver."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: "The Return of Jerry Lee" Single (1958)
facts.body: In an attempt by Sun Records to both capitalize on and defuse the controversy surrounding Jerry Lee Lewis's scandalous marriage, Jack Clement produced a novelty record. This single, a joke initially for Sun staff, featured DJ George Klein interviewing Lewis about the controversy, with Lewis's answers spliced from his existing records. Sam Phillips, despite its origins as a joke, insisted on releasing it. However, the record, which included "leering jokes about Myra's physical attractiveness," failed to defuse the situation and was criticized for its exploitation of a child. "Unsurprisingly, that did not have the effect that was hoped, and did not defuse the situation one Iota."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Creative Explosion in Greenwich Village (1958)
facts.body: After firing Norman Petty and being cut off financially, Holly moved to Greenwich Village with Maria Elena and experienced a massive creative surge, writing dozens of acoustic demos and planning ambitious projects including a Latin music album, gospel duets with Mahalia Jackson, and soul duets with Ray Charles. He also enrolled in Lee Strasberg's Actor's Studio to study method acting. "He was not only writing songs himself, but he was busily planning to make an album of Latin music, and he was making preparations for two more projects he'd like to do. An album of duets on gospel songs with Mahalia Jackson, and an album of sold duets with Ray Charles."

facts.title: Petty's Contract Deception (1958)
facts.body: Norman Petty revealed that Holly had actually been recording for Petty's company, not Brunswick or Coral, meaning all royalties went to Petty, and the Crickets' supposed bank account was empty. This financial revelation occurred while Maria Elena was pregnant, forcing Holly to undertake the "Winter Dance Party" tour. "By the terms of buddy's contract, he hadn't really been recording for Buns Recall Coral, so they didn't tell him a penny."

facts.title: Marketing Collaboration with Dick Clark (1958)
facts.body: Sun Records collaborated with Dick Clark on a major promotional campaign for Jerry Lee Lewis's single "Breathless." This involved offering signed copies of the record in exchange for five Beach Nut chewing gum wrappers and 50 cents for postage and packing. The campaign was highly successful, leading to gum shortages in some areas and the distribution of over 38,000 singles. Sun Records purchased an autograph stamp and hired temporary staff to manage the demand, splitting profits with Dick Clark. "Judd Phillips, Sam's brother, came up with a great promotional scheme."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Sam Phillips' Reign Ends (1958)
facts.body: Following the scandal surrounding Jerry Lee Lewis's marriage and the subsequent collapse of his career, combined with the departure of other major acts like Johnny Cash and Karl Perkins, Sam Phillips' brief but significant reign as "the most important record producer and company owner in the USA was over." Phillips continued to run Sun Records for a few more years before selling it. "With Jerry Lee Lewis's career destroyed, and with all his other major acts having left him, Phillips's brief reign as the most important record producer and company owner in the USA was over."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Planned UK Tour Failure (1958)
facts.body: Following the massive success of "Ma, He's Making Eyes at Me" in the UK, plans were made for a Johnny Otis Show tour of the country in 1958. However, these plans fell through due to the mutual protectionist agreement between the American Federation of Musicians and the British Musicians Union, which required a "like for like swap" of musicians for tours. Otis's band could not find an appropriate British counterpart for the exchange. "Those plans failed, because of something I've not mentioned in this podcast before, but which radically shaped British music culture, and to a lesser extent American music culture for decades."

facts.title: Conditions for Rejoining Elvis and Permanent Departure (1958)
facts.body: After his initial resignation and Elvis's attempt to replace him, Bill Black was offered his job back, with a per diem arrangement. However, after the very next recording sessions, Bill Black never again recorded with Elvis, being replaced by Bob Moore in the studio. Unlike Scotty Moore, Bill Black never worked with Elvis again after Elvis joined the army, choosing to focus on his own career. "But after the next recording sessions, Bill never again recorded with Elvis."

facts.title: Decline by 1958
facts.body: By 1958, Hank Ballard and the Midnighters were largely a forgotten group. Their R&B style, rooted in the LA sound pioneered by Johnny Otis, had been superseded by newer sounds from Memphis, Chicago, and New York. They had not had a hit in three years and were concerned about being dropped by their record label. "By 1958 though, they were largely a forgotten group."

facts.body: Brian Wilson drew direct inspiration from this song, specifically its melody and the opening verse's distinctive recitation of place names, which he subsequently adapted for The Beach Boys' "Surfin' USA." Due to the pronounced similarities, Chuck Berry was awarded the sole songwriting credit for "Surfin' USA," a decision that proved financially advantageous for him as "Surfin' USA" became a perennial oldies hit, unlike "Sweet Little Sixteen" itself. "Brian Wilson had been inspired by Chuck Berry's sweet little 16, and in particular the opening verse, which had just listed a lot of places."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Recorded at the same session as "Real in a Rockin'," this song captured the experience of being a rock and roll fan, moving beyond just dancing to music to describe fandom as a major part of life. While it contains elements of the "teen girl fan filtered through the male gaze," its strength lies in verses where the girl becomes the viewpoint character, expressing excitement for shows and her collections. The song famously name-checks "American Bandstand" and its location, Philadelphia. "Sweet Little Sixteen was one of the first songs about the experience of being a rock and roll fan."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Shared Musical Taste with Elvis (c. 1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller shared a mutual admiration for Elvis Presley's work ethic in the studio and his taste in blues music, which initially formed a strong basis for their creative collaboration. "They liked Elvis himself a lot, and they admired and respected his work ethic in the studio, and shared his taste in blues music."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Leiber and Stoller

facts.title: Boredom with Elvis Film Routines (c. 1958)
facts.body: After contributing to a couple of Elvis's films, Leiber and Stoller grew bored with the repetitive and routine nature of writing songs for them. They perceived the process as merely filling "gaps" with similar types of songs, stifling their creative expression. "They were already, after a couple of films, getting bored with the routine nature of writing for Elvis's films."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Leiber and Stoller

facts.title: Loss of RCA Jobs and Shift to R&B Focus (Post-June 1958)
facts.body: Following their definitive split from working with Elvis, Leiber and Stoller soon lost their jobs at RCA. This enabled them to redirect their focus entirely to their work with R&B artists, including notable groups such as The Clovers, The Coasters, and The Drifters. "They soon lost their jobs at RCA, which left them to concentrate on their work with R&B artists, like the Clovers, the Coasters, and the Drifters."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Leiber and Stoller

facts.title: Elvis Continued to Record Their Songs (Post-1958)
facts.body: Even after their direct studio collaboration ceased, Elvis Presley continued to "keep an eye on their careers" and recorded many more of Leiber and Stoller's songs, although they were no longer commissioned to write material specifically for him. These later recordings included songs they had written for other artists like The Clovers and The Coasters. "He'd just never again have them write a song specifically for him."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Leiber and Stoller

facts.title: Ultimate Second Chance Hit
facts.body: Recorded and released as a single in 1958 when Brenda Mae Tarplay (Brenda Lee) was 13 years old, the song didn't chart until 1960, reaching number 14 after she became a teen idol. Due to prevailing trends against holiday music charting well, it couldn't crack the Top 10 even at the height of her fame. In the streaming era, it returned to the Hot 100 every Christmas starting in 2013, steadily gaining strength. In 2023, after four years of peaking at number two behind Mariah Carey, and aided by a new music video featuring the 78-year-old Brenda lip syncing to her 13-year-old vocals, it finally topped the Hot 100. This set multiple chart records: the longest climb to number one (65 years), Lee as the oldest chart topper ever (78), and the longest gap between number one hits (63 years). "Brenda Lee's rockin' around the Christmas tree is an inspiring comeback story."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Second-Chance Hits Edition Part 2
facts.name: Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree

facts.body: Released in 1958, this instrumental was highly influential for its tone and style. Link Wray achieved new sounds through experimentation with tunings, amplifiers, distortion, and tremolo. It was banned by numerous radio stations for sounding "too dangerous" and potentially inciting violence, and it prefigured the sound of surf music. "Not only would this instrumental become very influential in terms of tone and style, but it was also banned by a bunch of radio stations because it sounded too dangerous and might incite listeners to violence."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Surf Music
facts.name: Rumble

facts.body: This instrumental piece, released in 1958, lacked lyrics or an explicit message, instead featuring a slow, dirty, and raw guitar sound. It utilized a distortion that was unprecedented in its aggression on commercial radio at the time. Its title, "Rumble," referred to street gang fights, a piece of youth slang from the 1950s, which was controversial in a musical landscape dominated by doo-wop and clean ballads, becoming an anomaly that anticipated a part of rock and roll. "Su título, Rumble, hacía referencia a las peleas entre mandas callejeras, la jerga juvenil de los años 50."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)
facts.name: Rumble

facts.body: This instrumental track by Link Wray, released in 1958, was created by intentionally poking holes in the speaker cones of his amplifier to achieve a raspy, distorted sound. The song was so controversial for its time that it was banned by some radio stations, who feared it encouraged juvenile delinquency and gang fights. Its unique sound proved hugely influential, inspiring guitarists globally to seek ways to duplicate it. "This song was so sinister for its day that it was banned by some radio stations believing that it encouraged not just juvenile delinquency, but gangfights."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback
facts.name: Rumble

facts.body: This was Link Wray's first single, released in 1958, and was a fuzzy, distorted instrumental, highly unique for its era, predating fuzz pedals. Wray achieved its "dirty and dangerous sound" by poking holes in his amplifier's speaker, after initially experimenting with a composition titled "Oddball." "In 1958, he released his first single, which was a fuzzy, distorted instrumental, very unique for its day because it was recorded years before there was such a thing as a fuzz pedal for the guitar."

facts.body: Inspired by Jerry Butler's "For Your Precious Love," this slow-burn ballad was initially rejected by Sid Nathan at Federal Records, who threatened to drop Brown. Convinced it would be a hit, Brown recorded a demo with his own money and took it directly to radio stations, where it quickly became the most requested song. After Federal received orders for 25,000 copies, Nathan reluctantly agreed to properly record the song in a studio at the label's expense. "Try Me" became an even bigger hit than "Please Please Please," reaching number one on the R&B charts and number 48 on the pop charts. "Primee became an even bigger hit than please please please had and went to number one and the R&B charts and number 48 on the pop charts."

facts.title: Complex Artistic Attitude Towards Elvis's Work (c. 1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber, as half of the songwriting duo Leiber and Stoller, held a nuanced view of his work with Elvis. While he liked Elvis and respected his studio work ethic, he considered much of their output for Elvis, particularly film songs, to be "easy money" rather than "real art" in the way their R&B records were. "But at the same time, they didn't consider the work they were doing with Elvis to be real art, in the way they considered their R and B records to be."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Jerry Leiber

facts.title: Belief in Missed Artistic Potential with Elvis (c. 1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber expressed the conviction that with proper artistic freedom, he and Mike Stoller could have "made history" with Elvis. He believed that Elvis's management team was solely focused on financial gain, leading to a routine of producing generic songs for films that stifled creative ambition. "But the gist of it is that they believed that if they were given proper artistic freedom with Elvis, they could have made history, but that the people in his management team only wanted money."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Jerry Leiber

facts.title: Contemptuous Comparison of "Trouble" (1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber compared "Trouble," a song he co-wrote as a joke, to "Black Denim Trousers and Motorcycle Boots." He expressed a sense of "contempt" for the idea that only "Hell's Angels and Elvis Presley" would take such songs seriously, implying that Elvis's rendition of the bluesy track didn't sound "right" to him. "Leighbaugh later said of Trouble, comparing it to that song. The only people who were going to take them seriously are Hell's Angels and Elvis Presley."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: Jerry Leiber

facts.title: Pneumonia and Final Break with Elvis (June 1958)
facts.body: Jerry Leiber contracted pneumonia, which prevented him from traveling to an Elvis recording session in June 1958. This health issue, combined with Colonel Parker's insistence and Mike Stoller's defiant advice, ultimately led to the permanent separation of Leiber and Stoller from working in the studio with Elvis and writing songs specifically for him. "Jerry Leighbaugh got pneumonia and was unable to travel to a session."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Jerry Leiber

facts.body: An old folk song from Veracruz, Mexico, exemplary of the Son Haracho style, with its earliest known recording dating to 1939, though its existence may span centuries. Traditionally sung at weddings, its origins are obscure; while some claims suggest an origin in music made by slaves in Mexico, referencing the Ambamba tribe or a 17th-century Bamba Ria uprising, it is more likely that the title refers to the Spanish word "Bambolia" (to sway, swing, or wobble), given that the lyrics are primarily about a dance with nonsense elements. The song's tradition blends Spanish, indigenous, and African styles. Valens was initially hesitant to record it due to concerns about selling out his cultural background and his poor Spanish, but learned the lyrics phonetically from his aunt. Unusually, he recorded the vocal as an overdub, with Bob Keane whispering the lyrics to him. The arrangement differed significantly from earlier versions, making it the first record to successfully merge Latin and rock'n'roll styles into a cohesive whole. It utilizes the "three-cord trick" sequence (one-four-five-four) and became profoundly influential, inspiring countless garage bands and other notable records like "Hang on Sloopy" and "Twist and Shout." It reached number 22 on the charts. "La Bamba was the first record to make that chord sequence popular, and inspired thousands of garage bands."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: This song is described as the definitive 50s rock and roll song and was the only rock and roll track included on the Voyager probes' golden record, sent into space by NASA in the 1970s. Its introduction is one of the most well-known guitar parts in history, influencing many subsequent artists. The lyrics, initially intended as a message to Johnny Johnson, evolved to be about an idealized version of Berry himself, with the original version referring to a "coloured boy." "Johnny Be Good is so much the epitome of American post-war culture that when NASA sent a record into space on the Voyager probes in the 70s, it was the only rock and roll song included in the selection of audio."

facts.body: This song was the first ever written by Ian Sanwell, created as an angry response to an article in The Maldives Maker that declared Rock and Roll dead. Initially, it was placed on the B-side of the proposed single, largely due to a lack of better options, and was quickly recorded. During its recording, the main engineer left for the opera, leaving junior engineer Malcolm Addy to record the track. Addy, being young and understanding of rock and roll sound, produced a much louder, more resonant sound, akin to Sun Records, making a significant difference to the track. Jack Good later heard it and insisted Cliff perform it on "Oh Boy!", leading the record label to flip the single to make "Move It" the A-side. Cliff worked with Good for a full week on his performance, meticulously instructed on every movement and facial expression. It became an immediate hit upon his TV debut in September 1958, reaching number two in the charts. "That track was still intended for the B-side, until the point that Jack Good heard it."

facts.body: Inspired by the "Hand Jive" dance popularized on the British TV show "6-5 Special" and demonstrated by The Three Tons of Joy, Johnny Otis wrote this song. He incorporated the Bo Diddley rhythm, although he consistently claimed to have heard the rhythm from convicts on a chain gang before Bo Diddley recorded it. Despite Otis's intention to capitalize on his UK success and the dance's popularity, the song did not achieve commercial success in the UK. However, it became Otis's only Top 10 pop hit in the US, reaching number 9 on the pop charts and number 1 on the R&B charts, his first R&B Top 10 in six years. "But while William the Han Jive didn't have any success in the UK, in the US it became Otis's only Top 10 pop hit, and his first R&B Top 10 hit as a performer in six years, reaching number 9 on the pop charts, and number 1 on the R&B charts."

facts.body: An old Cajun song that Buddy Holly produced for Waylon Jennings's first ever session in September 1958. This version blended Cajun music with R&B, featuring Holly on guitar and King Curtis on saxophone. "It was Jennings's first ever session, and they turned out an interesting version of the old Cajun song, Joli Blanc, which had earlier been a hit from Moon Mulligan."

facts.title: Defiant Advice to Jerry Leiber (June 1958)
facts.body: When Jerry Leiber was incapacitated by pneumonia and Colonel Parker insisted on his presence at an Elvis session, Mike Stoller advised Leiber to defiantly tell Parker to "do something to himself," using strong language. This act of defiance was a contributing factor to the final severing of Leiber and Stoller's direct professional relationship with Elvis. "Leighbaugh asked Stuller what he should do, and Stuller said to tell him to do something to himself, using words that you can't use without being bumped into the adult section of the podcast directories."

facts.title: String Section Collaboration (1958)
facts.body: Buddy Holly recorded with the Dick Jacobs Orchestra in October 1958, utilizing a full string section. Dick Jacobs was responsible for quickly arranging "It Doesn't Matter Anymore," basing it on pizzicato violins. "In October 1958, Holly went into the studio with the Dick Jacobs Orchestra, with the intention of recording three songs"

facts.title: Koss SP3s – First Consumer Model (1958)
facts.body: John Koss, after developing a portable record player with a privacy switch that redirected audio to headphones, realized the potential for standalone consumer headphones. In 1958, he introduced the Koss SP3s, the first consumer-grade headphones specifically designed for private listening. This product was a "huge hit" and marked the beginning of widespread headphone adoption. "And so in 1958, the first standalone consumer grade headphones, the Koss SP3s, were introduced."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Big Picture Stuff: Part 2

facts.title: Monophonic (Mono) Sound (Pre-1958)
facts.body: Until 1958, all recordings were monophonic or mono, meaning they had only one audio channel with minimal sonic differentiation between instruments. "Until 1958, all recordings were monophonic or mono, meaning that there was just one channel and not much sonic differentiation between any of the instruments."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

facts.title: Stereophonic (Stereo) Sound (Post-1958)
facts.body: Stereophonic sound, introduced after 1958, utilizes two speakers with slightly different audio material to create an effect of depth and separation, aiming for realism as if performers are present. "One came stereophonic sound."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
